title: Al Hirt's band: great individuals who lack group sound
summary: Jernberg says Hirt's band has five outstanding soloists but does not play as an organized group, comparing it to rough, unarranged early bands.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: Yes, very good. I was trying to think of his name just last night, I think. He had a style of clarinet playing that was very, very nice, very soft and subdued, but very nice clarinet playing. He used to work at the old Apex Club on 35th Street. Yes, he was a very nice clarinet player. Yes. He was a clarinet player. But I'll say this. We'll get back to Johnny Dodds again. That guy was strictly a New Orleans jazz clarinet player, but brother, his instrument always sounded like a clarinet. Yeah. Always sounded like a clarinet and a good, fine clarinet tone, too. Those Teschmarkers and all the rest of those guys, you can have them. I'll take Johnny Dodds every time. And this clarinet player that's with Al Hurt, oh, he's very good. The little bell. Yeah, that little shrimp. Very good man on a clarinet. Oh, brother, he can get plenty of stuff out of a clarinet. Oh, he really gets it out. There are five very exceptional men in that outfit. But when they're all playing, it's like five individuals playing, not like a group sounding like one organized group. It sounds like five individuals, each playing individually. And they're all great performers. But when they're all playing at the same time, they should fit in together and they don't. Each one is an outstanding performer, really performing, but performing by himself with no, just going on, you know.
Well, you said that Louie and Oliver performed pretty much by themselves. That's right, the same way. How does it sound like an integrated band? And by integrated, I just mean it was.
Yeah. No, those bands in those days sounded pretty rough and, you know, there should have been just a little bit of refinement about the sound.

They were totally lacking in the way of an organized sound, you know, and just a little touch of refinement or a little touch of know-how in regarding to playing as a group. And that's what Al Hertz Band needs. They need to learn how to play as a group, not as individuals. But as individuals, brother, there's about five of them that are great. And of course, that takes in Al Hertz. Al Hertz and that clarinet player and the, oh, the drummer that he's got. He's tremendous, man. He is some drummer, that guy. Wonderful.
